title: Respectful Workplace: Harassment, Bystander Action and Psychological Safety
source: U.S. Equal Employment Opportunity Commission — Harassment
summary: Recognize harassment and disrespectful conduct, learn how to respond as a bystander, and build team habits that support psychological safety. You will also know how to route concerns to the person or area responsible.
body:
Recognize harassment and disrespectful conduct, learn how to respond as a bystander, and build team habits that support psychological safety. You will also know how to route concerns to the person or area responsible.

About this course

For all DHS and DSD employees, including supervisors, who want shared language and practical options for a respectful workplace. It does not replace HR, EOAD or legal advice. Lessons can be opened in any order. Examples are practice. Keep reflection notes without identifying coworkers or members of the public. This course supports learning; formal employment, accommodation, civil-rights, eligibility and licensing decisions stay with the person or area responsible.

Learning objectives

Distinguish the legal definition of harassment from the broader conduct standard in state respectful workplace policy.

Describe the five bystander strategies: distract, delegate, document, delay and direct.

Explain Amy Edmondson's definition of team psychological safety.

Identify the internal and external routes for raising respectful workplace, harassment and discrimination concerns.

Practice and reflection

Explain the distinction tested in each knowledge check.

Compare the responses to each practice case and the reasons behind them.

Complete the course job aid for a situation you choose.

Applying the learning

Find and save the current contact route for DHS EOAD, your HR business partner and the Employee Assistance Program. If you supervise, review with HR what your referral duty looks like in practice.

Lesson sequence

What harassment and a respectful workplace mean

Bystander action: the five Ds at work

Psychological safety as team practices

Reporting routes: route, do not investigate

Job aid

Respectful Workplace: Harassment, Bystander Action and Psychological Safety: practice guide

A reusable guide for a situation you choose

Use observable details rather than assigning motives.

Invite perspectives without requiring personal disclosure.

Keep learning separate from individual assessment or personnel decisions.

When you witness something

Check safety first, for the targeted person and for you.

Pick one of the five Ds: distract, delegate, document, delay or direct.

Check in afterward and ask what the person needs.

Never share notes or recordings without the targeted person's consent unless you are a supervisor with a duty to report.

Do not investigate. Route the concern.

If someone brings you a concern

Listen, thank them and avoid judging whether it is serious enough.

Explain honestly what you can and cannot keep confidential.

Share the routes: supervisor, HR, EOAD, union representative, Employee Assistance Program, and external agencies.

If you are a supervisor and it involves a protected class, refer to HR or EOAD promptly.

Watch for and route any retaliation.

Team habits that build safety

Ask for the strongest case against your own idea before deciding.

Thank people who raise concerns, in front of others.

Respond to unfamiliarity with information and a chance to change.

When something lands badly, the person with more power leads the repair.

Say what changed because someone spoke up.

Try the guide and revisit it

If someone brought you a concern tomorrow, would you know which route fits? What would you need to look up or ask so you feel prepared?

U.S. Equal Employment Opportunity Commission — Harassment
Supports the federal definition of harassment, the protected characteristics, the condition-of-employment and severe-or-pervasive standards, and the note that petty slights are usually not illegal. Federal enforcement positions change, so check current EEOC guidance for any formal question.
(https://www.eeoc.gov/harassment)

Supports the list of protected classes in employment under Minnesota law, including sexual orientation and gender identity, and the reprisal protection. Formal determinations rest with MDHR and the courts.
(https://mn.gov/mdhr/yourrights/mhra/)

Minnesota Management and Budget — HR/LR Policy 1432, Respectful Workplace (revised 2023)
Supports the statewide definition of respectful conduct, examples of disrespectful behavior, the separation from protected-class harassment, and reporting routes including supervisor, HR, union representative and EAP.
(https://mn.gov/mmb-stat/policies/1432-respectful-workplace-policy.pdf)

Minnesota Management and Budget — HR/LR Policy 1436, Harassment and Discrimination Prohibited (revised 2024)
Supports examples of protected-class harassment including deliberate misgendering and name mispronunciation, supervisor duty to report immediately, and the retaliation prohibition.
(https://mn.gov/mmb-stat/policies/1436-harassmentdiscriminationprohibited.pdf)

Supports that supervisors refer complaints to the Equal Opportunity and Access office and do not investigate. This public copy is an older version that uses a prior office name; learners should confirm current procedures on the DHS intranet.
(https://mn.gov/dhs/assets/discrimination-harassment-retaliation_tcm1053-646912.pdf)

title: Building psychological safety on teams

About this course

For leaders, supervisors, and team leads improving team learning and decision practices. Teams need information that people may hesitate to share: a missing assumption, a mistake, a question, or a concern about a proposed decision. This course uses that concept to examine a service-review team. Leaders practice inviting useful input, responding constructively, learning from errors, and checking whether concerns reach decisions. The course does not promise that every idea will be accepted or every difficult conversation comfortable. title: Psychological safety and repair: practices, not personality
summary: People speak up when doing so is safe and useful. That safety comes from practices others can see: how disagreement is handled, how mistakes are treated, who carries repair, and whether input changes anything.
body: Psychological safety and repair: practices, not personality People speak up when doing so is safe and useful. That safety comes from practices others can see: how disagreement is handled, how mistakes are treated, who carries repair, and whether input changes anything. DSD staff described limited psychological safety, performance pressure, and doubt that their input changes decisions. Those are practice problems with practice answers. Invite disagreement before deciding, including questions about your own proposal. Acknowledge the contribution in a way that respects the person's preferences and the sensitivity of the concern. Public recognition may be welcome, but should not expose a person who raised a private concern. Respond to the concern and its impact before assuming intent. Clarify what happened and what support is needed within your role. A lack of knowledge may call for explanation and learning, but it does not erase harm or determine whether a formal reporting process applies. Put repair on the person with more power. When a comment or decision lands badly, the leader names it and takes responsibility for repair. The person harmed should not have to explain, educate, or forgive on a schedule. Show that input changed something. Every month, say what changed because someone spoke up. If nothing did, say why. Watch the grind. Constant urgency silences people. Protect time for thinking and for saying no. These practices do not replace established reporting processes. Use the appropriate Employee Culture, Human Resources, or civil-rights channel for complaints, harassment, or discrimination, and explain the applicable privacy limits. psychological safety repair team trust disagreement supervisor

title: The Fearless Organization: Creating Psychological Safety in the Workplace for Learning, Innovation, and Growth
summary: Amy Edmondson, a professor at Harvard Business School, has studied team learning for more than two decades and is the researcher most associated with the term "psychological safety." This book gathers her research into a single argument for leaders: people do their best work when they believe they can speak up, ask questions, admit mistakes, and disagree without being punished or humiliated. body:
The Fearless Organization: Creating Psychological Safety in the Workplace for Learning, Innovation, and Growth
Amy C. Edmondson
Amy Edmondson, a professor at Harvard Business School, has studied team learning for more than two decades and is the researcher most associated with the term "psychological safety." This book gathers her research into a single argument for leaders: people do their best work when they believe they can speak up, ask questions, admit mistakes, and disagree without being punished or humiliated. She shows what happens when that belief is absent and offers a toolkit for building it.
Psychological safety is a team-level belief that speaking up, questioning, and admitting error will not be punished.
It is distinct from niceness or low standards; the goal is high safety combined with high expectations.
Edmondson's hospital research showed that better teams reported more errors because they felt able to discuss them.
Fear is a poor motivator because it narrows thinking and causes people to withhold information leaders need.
Major corporate and public failures often trace back to people who saw a problem and stayed silent.
Candid organizations such as Pixar are demanding, not comfortable; candor is the mechanism of quality.
Leaders set the stage by framing work as uncertain and tying it to purpose.
Leaders invite participation through humility, inquiry, and structured forums.
Leaders respond productively by appreciating input, destigmatizing failure, and still sanctioning clear violations.
The leader's reaction to the first person who speaks up shapes whether anyone else will.
Psychological safety is a precondition for inclusion work: staff from underrepresented groups bear the highest cost for speaking up, so a climate that punishes candor silences them first. Human-services supervisors can use the toolkit to run case reviews and incident debriefs that surface problems rather than hide them, which matters directly for client safety. HR teams can add the survey items to engagement measures. A common critique is that the concept has been diluted into a buzzword and that Edmondson's framework says little about how power and identity shape who feels safe. Her later writing addresses this, but practitioners should layer an equity lens on top.
Where in your organization would a staff member hesitate before reporting an error, and what would it cost the client if they stayed silent?
Which of the three toolkit areas is weakest in your team's leadership practice?
Do staff from different identity groups experience the same level of safety on your team, and how would you find out?

title: 3. Speaking up, psychological safety and accountability
summary: Can people raise a concern, and what does the organization do when they do?
body:
3. Speaking up, psychological safety and accountability
Can people raise a concern, and what does the organization do when they do?
Describe psychological safety as a team's experience of speaking up, not a guarantee of comfort or agreement.
Respond to concerns without retaliation, promises of secrecy the leader cannot keep, or pressure to disclose private details.
Separate supportive words from a documented process that people can use and trust.
People may hesitate to ask a question, report a mistake or challenge a decision when they fear humiliation or consequences. Psychological safety concerns the shared belief that interpersonal risks such as speaking up are possible. Inviting feedback is a beginning; people also notice whether a leader listens, acts, shares credit and responds fairly afterward.
Cultural safety, workplace psychological safety and organizational safety culture are related but different. A person's experience of respect and power, a team's ability to raise concerns, and the organization's systems for reporting and responding each need attention. Do not assume one survey or training session measures all three.
Use existing reporting and accommodation channels when a concern involves a person's rights or safety. Explain what you can keep private, what you must route to a person or area responsible, and what will happen next. Avoid asking colleagues to make personal disclosures or to carry the work of educating others because of their identities.
In a team meeting, a staff member says the notice may be inaccessible and that a previous concern was ignored. A supervisor is worried about the deadline; a manager and director oversee the work and its resources. Another colleague interrupts, saying the meeting is not the place to question the plan.
Practice a response that thanks the person, stops interruption and names an immediate next step without promising confidentiality you cannot guarantee.
Offer more than one accessible way to contribute, including a private route when appropriate. Clarify who will evaluate the concern and when the team will hear back.
Record the process and decision without unnecessary personal details. Afterward, ask whether people could raise concerns and whether the process changed.
What evidence would show that raising a concern changed the response—not just that the supervisor said the door was open?

Psychological Safety, Respect, and Speaking Up
Examining how responses to questions, uncertainty, and mistakes can support useful learning while keeping responsibility clear.
Foundation self-directed learning
A relevant question can improve a service or a shared task, yet asking it may carry a social risk. Someone may fear appearing unprepared, challenging a senior colleague, or losing an opportunity. Psychological safety concerns that interpersonal risk in the team’s work. This course uses DSD situations to examine questions, mistakes, and follow-through. You will consider responses that make uncertainty easier to discuss and examine without promising immunity or removing standards. Your reflections can remain private, and no disclosure of a personal experience is required.
What does the first response teach?
A colleague asks, “Could this instruction leave someone without a usable route?” The reply is, “We have already discussed that.”

What is known about the instruction? What is known about the response?

Consider whether the reply answers the question or only discourages asking it again.
The earlier discussion may have addressed the concern, but the reply does not explain how. The colleague may need a reference, a correction, or a clearer answer. Notice the difference between stating that a discussion occurred and showing what it established. If questions repeatedly receive a dismissive reply, people may become less willing to supply relevant uncertainty. That is a possible mechanism, not proof of everyone’s experience. Begin with the specific response and the work question it leaves open.
Safety for interpersonal risk
Psychological safety describes a shared belief that a team is safe for interpersonal risk, such as asking, disagreeing, or acknowledging a mistake.

It is not constant comfort, friendship, or lower standards.

A respectful response can examine a claim without agreeing with it or judging the person’s worth.
Amy Edmondson’s work distinguishes a team condition from an individual personality trait. The question is how the team responds when someone takes an ordinary work risk, not whether that person is naturally confident. A pleasant meeting does not settle the issue if relevant concerns become unwelcome. Nor does a difficult conversation automatically mean learning is impossible. Keep the task evidence and responsibilities clear. A response can be demanding about the work while leaving a genuine route to ask, clarify, and correct.
A service concern before a decision
An employee notices a possible access gap in a draft but expects to be called disruptive for questioning an experienced colleague.

If the question remains unheard, the gap may continue. Repetition can privilege established voices over relevant evidence.

Receive the specific concern and examine the instruction through the appropriate review.
The employee’s concern may be accurate, partly accurate, or mistaken. The team cannot learn which if the social cost prevents the question from reaching review. A useful response separates the concern from a judgment about loyalty or competence. Ask which instruction creates the difficulty and what evidence could clarify it. The next case asks how to make the issue easier to examine without assuming the gap is proven or claiming that a friendly invitation alone has removed every reason to hesitate.
Practice: a service question
A staff member questions whether an instruction leaves a usable access route. A senior colleague replies, “We already discussed it.” Which response best supports useful learning?
A. Treat the concern as correct without checking the instruction.
B. Ask about the specific gap, examine the instruction, and explain the finding.
C. Tell the employee to be more confident before raising questions.
In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.
The employee has raised a question about a service instruction. Their status does not establish whether the concern is accurate. Compare how each alternative handles both the evidence and the social cost of asking. Automatic agreement avoids inquiry, while confidence advice can place all responsibility on the questioner. A stronger response examines the specific gap and explains what the review supports. Repeating that practice may make relevant knowledge more usable across differences in experience or position. It cannot establish that everyone now feels safe, and the instruction may still require another responsible reviewer or additional evidence.
The cost of asking is not identical
Position, earlier responses, visibility, and access to support can affect how risky a question feels.

Do not infer an employee’s confidence or experience from silence alone.

Consider the invitation and response conditions as well as the person’s observable behavior.
A senior employee and a newcomer can hear the same invitation differently because their position and earlier experience differ. That does not establish a universal rule about either person. Ask what conditions make a relevant question usable: clear purpose, enough context, and a response that examines its substance. Repeatedly asking only the least secure person to be braver can leave those conditions unchanged. Individual choice still matters, but it is not the whole explanation for whether useful knowledge reaches the team.
A precise question helps the work
Name the observation, explain its possible task consequence, and ask what needs clarification.

“This instruction names no contact” is easier to examine than “Nobody cares.”

Precision supports inquiry; it should not become a requirement to speak perfectly before a concern can be heard.
A specific question gives the discussion something concrete to examine. It can identify a missing step and ask which source supplies it. That is different from claiming a motive for everyone involved. At the same time, a person under pressure may not phrase a concern neatly. Receive the substance and ask a clarifying question without turning eloquence into an entry condition. The goal is to make uncertainty workable, not to demand a polished performance as proof that someone deserves a response.
Receive the question before defending intent
Acknowledge what was raised and examine the relevant evidence.

An intention to help does not answer whether the instruction or response worked.

Explain the finding, any correction, and what remains unresolved without asking the colleague to reassure you.
A question about your work can feel personal. Pausing to identify its actual substance can protect the relationship and improve the task. You might say that the contact instruction needs checking and explain who can review it. You do not have to agree that an error occurred before examining it. If you respond only by defending your good intention, the practical concern can disappear. Repeated use of that defense may teach colleagues that feedback mainly creates a need to comfort the receiver.
Disagreement and disrespect are different
A colleague can challenge a conclusion respectfully and contribute to a stronger decision.

Examine the evidence and the way the exchange occurred as distinct questions.

Ordinary learning does not replace the current route for a conduct concern, support need, or required report.
A team needs room to question an interpretation without treating disagreement itself as misconduct. It also needs appropriate conduct and actual concern processes. Do not collapse those responsibilities into one judgment that every uncomfortable exchange is harmful or every task-focused exchange is acceptable. Look at the specific words, context, and work evidence. If a concern requires a formal route, a practice conversation cannot delay it or decide the final finding. This learning course supports everyday responses while leaving those responsibilities intact.
A newcomer’s question becomes a warning
A newcomer asks how two instructions fit together. The reply is, “Everyone else understands; stop overthinking.”

The confusion may remain, and future questions may carry more risk. Repetition can turn missing context into a lasting ability judgment.

Clarify the instructions and consider the question’s work value.
The response compares the employee with others without showing that the instructions are consistent. It can leave both the task uncertainty and the social cost unresolved. If later feedback relies on this exchange, the newcomer may be seen as incapable rather than as someone who identified a gap. A clearer answer can preserve the necessary expectation while making it understandable. The upcoming choice asks how to respond to the actual question, not how to promise that every future interaction will feel safe.
Practice: uncertainty in onboarding
A newcomer asks how two instructions fit together. The reply is “Everyone else understands.” Which response better preserves learning and the work expectation?
A. Ask which instructions conflict and clarify the actual requirement.
B. Remove every requirement so the newcomer never feels uncomfortable.
C. Record the question as proof that the newcomer lacks ability.
In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.
The question concerns two instructions, so begin there. They may conflict, explain different conditions, or need a clearer connection. A useful response examines that possibility without treating uncertainty as evidence that the employee cannot do the work. Neither lower standards nor a permanent label follows from the account. Think about how an early response could shape later feedback: if the confusion is recorded only as an ability problem, future opportunities may narrow while the original instruction remains unclear. The stronger response makes the requirement usable and considers the actual evidence, leaving broader judgments for their appropriate process.
Different ways to raise a useful question
A spoken question, prepared note, or appropriate written follow-up can serve a task differently.

Explain the purpose and real timing so staff know how a contribution can still matter.

A familiar speaking style should not become the only evidence of engagement.
Some work requires an immediate decision, while other questions can be considered after preparation. Make that distinction visible. A person who develops a careful written question may be contributing thoughtfully, not avoiding the work. A direct question can also express care without being a personal attack. Find an arrangement that meets the actual need rather than assuming one style is universally best. If only quick speech is recognized, relevant knowledge may stay outside the discussion and later judgments about engagement may narrow.
A mistake needs a present response
Identify the error, address its current consequence through the proper role, and examine how it happened.

Learning about conditions does not erase responsibility.

Shame can conceal useful information; reassurance without correction can leave the actual problem unresolved.
A mistaken date in a service message may need an immediate correction. Examining the draft process can also help explain how the date entered and escaped review. Keep both needs visible. Calling the employee careless may conceal a confusing source or missed review step; saying that mistakes never matter may ignore the effect on readers. A thoughtful response attends to the current problem and then asks a specific learning question. It does not promise immunity or replace any applicable formal responsibility.
Repair your own response specifically
If you dismissed a question, acknowledge that response and return to the unanswered work issue.

An apology can matter without settling what the colleague experienced.

If the judgment entered a note or later decision, consider the appropriate route to correct that account too.
You can say that your reply cut off a relevant question and explain how it will now receive an answer. That is more useful than asking the colleague to confirm that everything is fine. Consider where the original interpretation traveled. A private change of mind may not address a lasting label in a work account. Use the appropriate responsibility to correct what can be corrected. Keep the scope specific: repair can improve one exchange while the person’s wider experience and future confidence remain unknown.
Community listening also involves risk
People using services may weigh what happens if they question an instruction or disagree with staff.

Explain the purpose, available choices, and appropriate route for questions.

A culture brief can prepare inquiry; the person’s current account supplies knowledge of this experience.
An invitation to comment can carry unequal influence even when the staff member intends to listen. A person may be unsure whether disagreement affects the service relationship. Give an honest explanation of the purpose and the actual arrangements rather than making guarantees you cannot support. Hear the particular question and respond within your role. A brief may help you notice context, but it cannot predict what every participant fears or prefers. Ask what would make this contribution usable without requiring personal disclosure.
When a public question receives a rebuke
At a community discussion, someone asks about an unclear route and is told they should have read the website.

The route may still be unclear. Repeated rebukes can suppress the very knowledge needed to improve it.

Receive the specific question and explain what can be checked or clarified.
The website might contain the answer, but the reply does not establish whether the person could find or use it. Asking about the particular route can reveal a missing instruction, a difficult format, or a misunderstanding that a clear explanation resolves. Do not promise that every aspect of the process can change. Identify the actual scope and provide a useful response. The next choice examines how staff can learn from the question without treating one participant as the voice of everyone or blaming the person for an unexamined gap.
Practice: a question from a service user
At a community discussion, a participant asks about a route and hears “You should have read the website.” What response is more useful?
A. Ask the person to prove they read every page before answering.
B. Invite one participant to speak for the whole community.
C. Clarify the question, check the route, and explain what can be answered or reviewed.
In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.
The participant may have read the page and still found the route unclear, or may need a different way to reach the information. The reply does not distinguish those possibilities. Ask about the specific question and examine what the available instruction actually explains. A stronger response gives a useful answer or identifies what needs review, with honest limits about authority and timing. A culture brief may help prepare attention to different experiences with institutions; it cannot answer for the participant. Keep the person’s account within its scope and avoid making disclosure or perfect preparation the price of being heard.
An invitation needs follow-through
Asking for questions is a beginning. Consider whether the question received an answer and whether the answer addressed its substance.

A friendly acknowledgment can still leave the gap unresolved.

Explain what was checked, what changed if anything, and where another responsibility is needed.
A team can sincerely thank someone and still fail to act on the information they supplied. Follow the route from invitation to question, response, and finding. Each step tells you something different. If the response is unavailable yet, say what remains to be examined rather than implying the concern disappeared. Repeated unanswered invitations may discourage later contribution. Thoughtful follow-through does not require agreeing with every suggestion; it requires a useful account of how the relevant question was considered.
Evidence is not a safety ranking
A completed answer or corrected instruction is a work result. A person’s voluntary account describes their experience.

Silence, attendance, or fewer questions cannot by themselves establish psychological safety.

Do not rank employees’ courage, loyalty, or intercultural development from course choices.
The course can help you practice reasoning about a response. It cannot certify a team’s psychological safety or diagnose an employee. Keep work evidence and personal experience distinct. You may know a concern received an answer while not knowing whether the person felt able to raise another one. Fewer questions could mean clearer instructions, less opportunity, or reluctance to ask. Identify the evidence needed for the actual question and avoid replacing that inquiry with a reassuring score based on limited observations.
Rewrite the first reply
Use the sentence: “Everyone else understands.”

Write a response that clarifies the instruction and invites the relevant question without removing the work expectation.

What repeated consequence could the original reply create for a newcomer?
A possible revision asks which two instructions seem inconsistent and offers to examine the difference. It keeps the employee responsible for the work while making the expectation usable. Compare that with the original reply, which can turn uncertainty into a personal comparison. If repeated, the response may discourage questions and allow unresolved gaps to shape later performance impressions. Your reflection can remain private. The aim is a more specific, useful exchange, not a script that guarantees every conversation will go well.
Respect includes the right route
An everyday response can support learning. A formal concern may need another process or responsible role.

Do not require confrontation, personal disclosure, or a team exercise before someone uses an applicable route.

Do not investigate another person’s allegation or promise confidentiality beyond your actual responsibility.
A supportive conversation and an appropriate formal route can coexist. Someone may need clarification of a task, an individual support arrangement, or a response to a serious conduct concern. Listen without requiring them to classify the matter perfectly first. Use current agency guidance for the actual situation and keep information within the proper handling. This course does not provide an investigation or a finding. Respecting that boundary helps avoid turning ordinary learning into a gate that delays the responsibility a concern requires.
Keep questions useful and responsibility clear
Psychological safety concerns the risk of asking, disagreeing, and acknowledging uncertainty in shared work.

Receive the substance, examine evidence, and follow through without shame or unsupported reassurance.

Continue with respectful workplace learning and inclusive supervision when further support is useful.
You have examined how a response can make relevant uncertainty easier to consider or harder to raise. Keep the work question visible, especially when experience or status differs. A respectful response does not need to agree in advance, remove a standard, or promise complete safety. It can provide a meaningful route to an answer while retaining the appropriate responsibility. Listen after making a change, state what remains unknown, and use actual formal processes when the issue calls for them.

title: What harassment and a respectful workplace mean
summary: Distinguish the legal definition of harassment from the broader conduct standard in state respectful workplace policy.
body:
Distinguish the legal definition of harassment from the broader conduct standard in state respectful workplace policy.

What harassment and a respectful workplace mean

People use the word harassment loosely, so it helps to separate three layers. The first is the law. The U.S. Equal Employment Opportunity Commission describes harassment as unwelcome conduct based on a protected characteristic such as race, color, religion, sex, national origin, age forty and older, disability or genetic information. Under federal law it becomes illegal when putting up with it becomes a condition of keeping the job, or when it is severe or pervasive enough that a reasonable person would find the workplace intimidating, hostile or abusive. The EEOC is clear that petty slights and isolated incidents, unless extremely serious, usually do not reach that legal line.

The second layer is Minnesota law. The Minnesota Human Rights Act protects more groups than federal law does. The Minnesota Department of Human Rights lists race, religion, disability, national origin, sex, marital status, familial status, age, sexual orientation and gender identity among the protected classes, and the Act also prohibits reprisal against people who assert their rights. Age protection under state law starts at the age of majority rather than at forty.

The third layer is state and agency policy, and this is where most everyday conduct is addressed. Minnesota Management and Budget sets statewide human resources policies for executive branch agencies. Its Harassment and Discrimination Prohibited policy covers unwelcome conduct tied to protected class, including offensive jokes, slurs, and deliberate misgendering or mispronunciation of a name. Its Respectful Workplace policy covers disrespectful conduct that is not tied to protected class: shouting, threats, demeaning or humiliating treatment, bullying, and sabotaging someone's work. DHS has its own policies that follow the same pattern. Policy standards are deliberately set below the legal line, so an employer can correct behavior before it becomes a legal problem.

Here is the practical point. You do not have to decide whether something is illegal harassment, a policy violation or just a bad day before you raise it. Sorting that out is the job of Human Resources and the DHS Equal Opportunity and Access Division. Your job is to notice, to respond in a way that is safe, and to route the concern to people who can act. This course builds shared language for doing that. It does not make anyone an investigator or a legal decision-maker.

Law sets the floor, policy sets a higher standard for daily conduct, and you do not need to classify a concern before raising it. Classification belongs to HR and EOAD.

Concepts to carry forward

Prompt

Harassment (legal)

Explanation

Unwelcome conduct based on a protected characteristic that becomes a condition of employment or is severe or pervasive enough to create a hostile work environment.

Prompt

Respectful workplace policy

Explanation

Statewide and DHS policy covering disrespectful conduct such as shouting, bullying and demeaning treatment, including conduct that is not tied to a protected class.

Prompt

The five Ds

Explanation

Distract, delegate, document, delay and direct: five bystander options taught by Right To Be. Choose the one that is safe and fits what the targeted person wants.

Prompt

Psychological safety

Explanation

Edmondson's term for a shared belief that a team is safe for interpersonal risk taking, such as asking questions, admitting mistakes or disagreeing.

Prompt

Retaliation

Explanation

Negative treatment of someone because they reported, opposed or took part in an investigation of harassment or discrimination. It is prohibited.

Prompt

EOAD

Explanation

The DHS Equal Opportunity and Access Division, which receives and investigates discrimination, harassment and retaliation complaints.

A practice example to examine

Practice case: In a DSD policy team meeting, Corwin keeps calling a coworker, Ilse, by a shortened nickname she has asked him not to use. He jokes that her full name is too hard. Later, in a message thread, he mocks her accent. Ilse's teammate Marguerite notices both. Marguerite is not sure whether this counts as harassment or just rudeness, and she worries that if she calls it harassment and is wrong, she will look like she is overreacting.

Practice and review

Find the current DHS respectful workplace and harassment and discrimination policies on the DHS intranet or through your HR contact. Note in your own words one example of conduct each policy names, and where each policy says to report.

Private reflection

Think about a time you hesitated to name something at work because you were not sure it was serious enough. What would have helped you feel able to raise it without first having to judge it?

Check your understanding

Why do state respectful workplace and harassment policies reach conduct that may not be illegal?

Option 1: So the employer can address and correct harmful conduct early, before it becomes severe or pervasive.

Option 2: Because state policy replaces federal law for state employees.

Option 3: Because every rude comment is illegal under the Minnesota Human Rights Act.

Answer review

Correct response: So the employer can address and correct harmful conduct early, before it becomes severe or pervasive.

Feedback for the correct response

Policy is intentionally set above the legal floor. It lets supervisors, HR and EOAD address conduct early. It does not replace federal law, and not every rude act is illegal. The value of the policy is that you can raise a concern without proving a legal case.

Feedback for another response

The second layer is Minnesota law.

The third layer is state and agency policy, and this is where most everyday conduct is addressed.

Later, in a message thread, he mocks her accent. Ilse's teammate Marguerite notices both. Marguerite is not sure whether this counts as harassment or just rudeness, and she worries that if she calls it harassment and is wrong, she will look like she is overreacting.

What is the most useful way for Marguerite to think about what she saw?

Option 1: Wait until she is certain the conduct meets the legal definition of harassment before saying anything.

Response to this choice

The legal line is not the threshold for raising a concern. Policy reaches conduct well below it, and waiting for certainty usually means waiting too long.

Option 2 — recommended response: Recognize that the conduct may fall under state policy whether or not it is illegal, and that she can raise it without deciding which category it fits.

Response to this choice

This is the best response. Deliberately mispronouncing a name and mocking an accent are examples the state policies name. Marguerite can describe what she saw and let HR or EOAD determine how it is classified.

Option 3: Decide it is only rudeness, since one nickname and one joke are isolated incidents.

Response to this choice

Repeated conduct after a request to stop is not an isolated incident, and conduct linked to national origin may fall under the harassment policy. Deciding it is minor on Ilse's behalf is not Marguerite's call.

title: Bystander action: the five Ds at work
summary: Describe the five bystander strategies: distract, delegate, document, delay and direct.
body:
Describe the five bystander strategies: distract, delegate, document, delay and direct.

Bystander action: the five Ds at work

Most harmful conduct at work happens in front of other people. Research and practice on bystander action start from a simple observation: people often want to help but freeze because they do not know what to do or fear making things worse. Right To Be, a national nonprofit that trains people to respond to harassment, teaches five options, known as the five Ds. Having more than one option matters, because the right response depends on safety, setting and what the targeted person wants.

Distract means interrupting the moment without confronting anyone. In a meeting, that might be changing the subject, asking the targeted person a work question, or calling a short break. Delegate means bringing in someone with more authority or a better position to act, such as a supervisor, a meeting chair or HR. Document means making a factual note of what happened: date, time, words used and who was present. Right To Be stresses that you should always ask the targeted person what they want done with any record, and never share it without their permission. In a state agency, remember that notes you create on state systems may be government data, so keep them factual and share them only through proper channels. Delay means checking in afterward: saying that what happened was not okay, asking what the person needs and offering to go with them to report. Direct means naming the behavior briefly, such as saying that comment was not okay, but only when it is safe and when direct action is likely to help rather than escalate.

Two limits are important. First, bystander action is not investigation. You are not gathering evidence, interviewing coworkers or deciding what happened. Second, supervisors carry an added duty. Statewide policy requires managers and supervisors to report protected-class harassment or discrimination they learn about to HR or the agency affirmative action officer, and DHS policy directs supervisors to refer complaints to the Equal Opportunity and Access Division. A supervisor can still distract or check in, but cannot agree to keep protected-class harassment secret.

Delay is often the most underused option. A quiet follow-up can reduce isolation, and the person who was targeted keeps control over what happens next.

There is always something you can do. Choose the option that is safe, fits the setting and respects what the targeted person wants, and route concerns rather than investigating them.

A practice example to examine

Practice case: During a video call with county partners, a DHS contractor named Garrick makes a joke about a program participant's religion. The DSD staff member who organized the call, Tamsin, sees her colleague Yusra go quiet with her camera off. Tamsin is not a supervisor. The call has twenty minutes left, and several partners are senior to her. Afterward, Tamsin wonders whether she missed her chance to do anything.

Practice and review

Write down two short phrases you could use in a meeting to distract or direct, and one sentence you could use to check in with a coworker afterward. Keep them somewhere you will see them before your next large meeting.

Private reflection

Which of the five Ds feels most natural to you, and which feels hardest? What would make the hardest one easier to use in your actual meetings?

Check your understanding

According to Right To Be, what should a bystander do with a recording or note of a harassment incident?

Option 1: Post it so others can see the behavior was witnessed.

Option 2: Ask the person who was targeted what they want done with it, and not share it without their permission.

Option 3: Keep it private and never mention it to anyone, including the person targeted.

Answer review

Correct response: Ask the person who was targeted what they want done with it, and not share it without their permission.

Feedback for the correct response

Documentation exists to support the person who was targeted. Sharing without consent can harm them and take away their choices. Keeping it secret from them also removes their choice. Supervisors have separate reporting duties under state policy.

Feedback for another response

What is the most helpful thing Tamsin can do now that the call is over?

Response to this choice

This is the best response. It uses delay, respects Yusra's control over next steps and opens a path to report. Because the speaker is a contractor, the contract manager and HR are appropriate routes for addressing his conduct.

Option 2: Email Garrick and the county partners describing the comment so everyone knows it was unacceptable.

Response to this choice

Public calling out in a group email can escalate, expose Yusra without her consent and bypass the people responsible for addressing contractor conduct.

Option 3: Record everything she remembers and forward it to HR right away without talking to Yusra.

Response to this choice

Making a factual note is reasonable, but sending it before speaking with Yusra removes her choice. Unless Tamsin is a supervisor with a duty to report, she should ask Yusra first.

title: Psychological safety as team practices
summary: Explain Amy Edmondson's definition of team psychological safety.
body:
Explain Amy Edmondson's definition of team psychological safety.

Psychological safety as team practices

Amy Edmondson, a researcher at Harvard Business School, defined team psychological safety as a shared belief held by members of a team that the team is safe for interpersonal risk taking. Interpersonal risks are ordinary work acts that could make someone look ignorant, incompetent or disruptive: asking a question, admitting a mistake, raising a concern or disagreeing with a more senior person. In her study of work teams in a manufacturing company, psychological safety was associated with more learning behavior, and learning behavior was associated with better team performance. That study, like much of the later research, shows association rather than proof that one causes the other, but the pattern has been repeated in many settings.

Psychological safety is not the same as being nice, avoiding conflict or lowering expectations. A team can hold high standards and still make it safe to say that something is not working. In fact, candor is what lets high standards be met. It is also a team-level condition. It describes how a group works, not a personality trait that some staff have and others lack.

Because it is a condition, it is built through practices that anyone can observe. Make disagreement normal: before deciding, ask for the strongest case against your own idea, and thank the person who raised a concern in front of others. Separate unfamiliarity from intentional harm: most awkward moments at work come from not knowing, and the right response is information and a chance to change. Intentional harm goes to the formal channels. Put repair on the person with more power: when a comment or decision lands badly, the leader names it and takes responsibility, and the person harmed is not asked to explain, educate or forgive on a schedule. Show that input changed something: regularly say what changed because someone spoke up, and if nothing did, say why. Watch the grind: constant urgency silences people, so protect time for thinking and for saying no.

None of this replaces the confidential and formal channels. A team with good habits still routes complaints of harassment and discrimination to HR and EOAD. Psychological safety makes it more likely people will speak up early. It does not make the supervisor an investigator.

Psychological safety is a shared belief that interpersonal risk is safe here. It is built by observable habits, especially how leaders respond to disagreement, mistakes and harm.

A practice example to examine

Practice case: Rosalind supervises a DSD waiver policy team. In a planning meeting, she dismisses a concern from a newer analyst, Obi, about a notice that he thinks will confuse families, saying there is no time to revisit it. Two weeks later a county partner raises the same problem. Rosalind notices that Obi has stopped speaking in meetings. She wants to fix the damage without making Obi feel singled out.

Private reflection

Option 1: A policy that guarantees no one will ever feel uncomfortable at work.

Option 2: A personality trait of confident employees who speak up easily.

Option 3: A shared belief among team members that the team is safe for interpersonal risk taking.

Answer review

Correct response: A shared belief among team members that the team is safe for interpersonal risk taking.

Feedback for the correct response

title: Reporting routes: route, do not investigate
summary: Identify the internal and external routes for raising respectful workplace, harassment and discrimination concerns.
body:
Identify the internal and external routes for raising respectful workplace, harassment and discrimination concerns.

Reporting routes: route, do not investigate

Knowing where to go is part of a respectful workplace. State and DHS policies give several routes, and a person can choose the one that feels safest. For respectful workplace concerns, statewide policy lists the employee's supervisor, the agency Human Resources office, a union representative and the Employee Assistance Program as places to start, and it encourages informal resolution where that is safe and appropriate. For harassment or discrimination tied to a protected class, statewide policy lists supervisors and managers, the agency affirmative action officer and the HR office. At DHS, the Equal Opportunity and Access Division handles discrimination, harassment and retaliation complaints. People can also go outside the agency to the Minnesota Department of Human Rights or the U.S. Equal Employment Opportunity Commission, which have their own filing deadlines.

Supervisors have a specific duty. Statewide policy requires managers and supervisors to report allegations of protected-class harassment or discrimination to HR or the affirmative action officer right away, and DHS policy directs supervisors to refer complaints to EOAD. DHS policy is also clear that supervisors do not investigate these complaints themselves. That means a supervisor should not interview witnesses, ask the person to prove what happened, confront the person accused, or try to mediate a protected-class complaint. Well-meant investigating can compromise a fair process, expose private data and put the person who raised the concern at risk. A supervisor's job is to listen, make sure the person is safe, refer promptly and keep the matter to people who need to know.

Retaliation is prohibited. Under state policy and the Minnesota Human Rights Act, no one may be punished for reporting, opposing harassment or discrimination, or taking part in an investigation. Retaliation can be obvious, like a worse assignment, or subtle, like being left out of meetings. Watch for it, and route it the same way.

Finally, be careful with information. Complaint information is sensitive. Share what is needed with the office that will act, keep your own notes factual, and do not discuss the matter with coworkers. If you are unsure which route fits, contact HR or EOAD and ask. Asking is never the wrong step.

Everyone can raise a concern through several routes. Supervisors listen, keep people safe and refer promptly to HR or EOAD. They never investigate protected-class complaints themselves.

A practice example to examine

Practice case: Anneliese, a DSD unit supervisor, is approached by Desmond, a case management consultant, who says a colleague has made repeated comments about his disability and has joked about his accommodation in front of others. Desmond asks Anneliese to keep it between them and just talk to the colleague informally. Anneliese wants to respect Desmond's wishes and fix the problem quickly.

Practice and review

Private reflection

If someone brought you a concern tomorrow, would you know which route fits? What would you need to look up or ask so you feel prepared?

Option 1: Because the person or area responsible conducts a fair process, and supervisor investigating can compromise it, expose private information and put the reporting employee at risk.

Option 2: Because supervisors are not allowed to listen to complaints at all.

Option 3: Because referral is only needed when the supervisor believes the complaint is true.

Answer review

Correct response: Because the person or area responsible conducts a fair process, and supervisor investigating can compromise it, expose private information and put the reporting employee at risk.

Feedback for the correct response

Supervisors should listen carefully and support the employee. What they do not do is determine what happened. Referral does not depend on whether the supervisor believes the account. The office responsible for investigation makes that determination.

Feedback for another response

Supervisors should listen carefully and support the employee. What they do not do is determine what happened. Referral does not depend on whether the supervisor believes the account. The office responsible for investigation makes that determination.

Key points

Supervisors have a specific duty.

Retaliation is prohibited.

Finally, be careful with information.

title: Understand what the team-learning concept does and does not mean
summary: Explain psychological safety as a team-learning concept.
body:
Explain psychological safety as a team-learning concept.

Colleagues share information and consider a decision together.

People should be able to question the work while the work still has standards.

Understand what the team-learning concept does and does not mean

Psychological safety concerns whether people expect that asking questions, raising concerns, or admitting mistakes will lead to humiliation or inappropriate punishment. It is a shared team expectation, rather than a label describing an individual’s courage or personality. Research connects the concept with learning behavior, but a leader cannot guarantee a particular outcome simply by announcing a safe space.

In a service-review team, a staff member questions whether a proposed form excludes people using assistive technology. The question may challenge the plan without attacking anyone. The team can examine it seriously and still decide that an idea needs further evidence or cannot be implemented as suggested.

Do not promise unlimited confidentiality, no accountability, or freedom from every uncomfortable discussion. Formal reporting and response duties continue. The leader’s practical role is to make useful questions possible, respond professionally, and keep decisions connected to evidence and authority rather than ridicule or unquestioning agreement.

In this lesson

1. Explain psychological safety as a team-learning concept.

2. Distinguish a useful disagreement from a guarantee of agreement or comfort.

3. Identify a formal responsibility that a team-learning promise cannot remove.

4. What should the leader explain instead?

People should be able to question the work while the work still has standards.

Key terms

Prompt

Psychological safety

Explanation

A team-learning concept concerning people’s expectation that they can raise questions, concerns, ideas, or mistakes without humiliation or inappropriate punishment.

Prompt

Interpersonal risk

Explanation

The possible social cost of asking for help, disagreeing, or admitting uncertainty in front of others.

Prompt

Invitation

Explanation

A practical opportunity to contribute, with a clear question, usable route, and enough time to respond.

Prompt

Constructive response

Explanation

A response that examines the content and next step without ridiculing the contributor.

Prompt

Learning review

Explanation

Examination of how work occurred and what should improve, separate from any required formal finding or accountability process.

Prompt

Follow-through

Explanation

Showing what happened to a contribution or concern and who is responsible for the next step.

Examine the decision

Team expectation

The issue is what people expect will happen when they take an interpersonal risk. A staff member may have useful knowledge but hesitate because earlier questions were mocked. Examine the team’s response practices rather than blame the person for insufficient confidence or assign an individual safety rating.

Standards

Clear standards can coexist with respectful questioning. In the form-review case, staff still need a usable and accurate product by an appropriate date. Inviting a concern about access does not waive those requirements; it gives the team information needed to meet them more reliably.

Boundaries

A team-learning promise cannot override complaint, records, or emergency responsibilities. If a report alleges discrimination, the leader must use the proper route rather than keep it inside an informal safe-space discussion. Explain limits honestly and distinguish learning conversation from formal action.

Check your understanding

Which statement correctly frames psychological safety?

Option 1: A team should support useful questions and concerns without humiliation while retaining standards and formal duties.

Option 2: Every idea must be adopted.

Option 3: No disagreement proves the team is safe.

Option 4: All reports can remain secret inside the team.

Answer review

Correct response: A team should support useful questions and concerns without humiliation while retaining standards and formal duties.

Feedback for the correct response

The framing connects speaking up to learning without removing judgment, accountability, or required processes.

Feedback for another response

Adopting every idea removes decision responsibility, and silence cannot prove that speaking up is possible. Absolute secrecy can also conflict with formal duties. Support professional questioning while keeping evidence, standards, and appropriate routes clear.

Compare the approaches

Agreement as safety

A meeting with no disagreement can feel smooth, but agreement does not establish that questions were possible. People may lack information or expect a negative response. Examine how input is invited and treated instead of using consensus as proof of a healthy process.

Questioning with standards

Questioning with standards makes the purpose and evidence clear while allowing uncertainty to be raised. It helps the team examine a real decision. An idea can be declined professionally when its substance is considered and the reason is explained.

No consequences promise

A promise of no consequences may sound welcoming, but can conflict with legitimate accountability and formal duties. State that people can raise concerns professionally and explain appropriate routes. Do not promise protections or secrecy beyond the leader’s authority.

Available categories

Learning concept

Relevant standard

False guarantee

Items to categorize

1. A person can raise a missing assumption without ridicule.

2. The team can ask for help when knowledge is incomplete.

3. The final form must be usable and accurate.

4. The proper complaint process remains available.

5. Every idea will be accepted.

6. No information will ever need another the person or area responsible.

Category: Relevant standard

Learning objective

Key points

The concept concerns the experience of speaking up.

It does not require accepting every idea or removing standards.

Practice and reflection

Practice includes a scenario choice, a knowledge check, a sorting activity, and a reflection. These activities do not establish that a change was used or that an outcome improved.

What should the leader explain instead?

Option 1: Keep the promises to make people comfortable.

Response to this choice

Option 2 — recommended response: Invite professional questions while explaining standards, authority, and formal privacy limits.

Option 3: Avoid all participation because the promises were too broad.

title: Invite useful input before the decision closes
summary: Write a focused invitation tied to a real decision uncertainty.
body:
Write a focused invitation tied to a real decision uncertainty.

Colleagues share information and consider a decision together.

An invitation needs a real opportunity, not just welcoming words.

Invite useful input before the decision closes

“Any questions?” is often too broad or too late to reveal an important concern. A useful invitation identifies what the team is deciding, what remains uncertain, and how people can respond before the choice closes. People may need preparation, a written route, or a smaller conversation to contribute relevant information.

In the practice form-review team, the leader asks for concerns after the design is sent for approval. A staff member had identified an access problem but did not interrupt the fast discussion. Providing the draft earlier and asking specifically about access barriers gives the concern a better chance to reach the decision.

Do not require every person to speak publicly or explain a personal experience. Offer appropriate routes and show how input will be considered. If the decision is already fixed, say what can still be influenced. An invitation that conceals its limits risks turning participation into ceremony rather than useful learning.

In this lesson

1. Write a focused invitation tied to a real decision uncertainty.

2. Identify a participation route that excludes a relevant contribution.

3. Plan more than one usable way to respond without requiring personal disclosure.

4. What should change?

An invitation needs a real opportunity, not just welcoming words.

Examine the decision

Question

Ask about a concrete uncertainty, such as what could prevent people from using the form. This gives staff a defined task and can surface information the leader lacks. A broad request for positivity or team agreement does not serve the same purpose because it discourages the very concern the decision needs.

Timing

Invite input while there is still a meaningful path to act on it. In the form-review case, a late question after submission makes correction harder. Share the material with enough appropriate preparation and identify the input deadline and decision responsibility without promising that every suggestion will be used.

Route

A written route or planned discussion can complement spoken input. The purpose is to capture relevant knowledge, not rank courage or force personal disclosure. Confirm that the route actually reaches the person reviewing the decision; an unread comment box is not a usable alternative.

Check your understanding

What makes the form-review invitation useful?

Option 1: Ask only after final submission.

Option 2: A focused access question, timely material, and a response route that reaches the decision.

Option 3: Require a personal story from each employee.

Option 4: Count silence as approval.

Answer review

Correct response: A focused access question, timely material, and a response route that reaches the decision.

Feedback for the correct response

The invitation gives relevant knowledge a usable path into a decision that can still respond.

Feedback for another response

Late timing, forced personal stories, and assumed approval all narrow meaningful participation. A useful invitation names the uncertainty, provides appropriate preparation, and explains how input reaches the decision without requiring disclosure.

Compare the approaches

Late broad invitation

A late broad invitation is easy to add to an agenda but may leave the decision effectively closed. It can make lack of response look like agreement. Identify what remains open and ask a focused question before the relevant review point.

Usable alternatives

Usable alternatives let people contribute through a route that fits the task and conditions. They require clear timing and review responsibility. A written comment route only helps when the team knows how the comments will reach the actual decision.

Forced disclosure

Forcing everyone to share a personal story can create pressure and collect information unnecessary to the decision. Invite evidence and perspectives without demanding an identity or experience narrative. People can contribute a practical concern without representing an entire group.

6. Everyone must disclose a personal experience to contribute.

title: Respond to a concern by examining its content
summary: Prepare a constructive response to a question that challenges a plan.
body:
Prepare a constructive response to a question that challenges a plan.

Colleagues share information and consider a decision together.

The response tells the team whether the invitation was real.

Respond to a concern by examining its content

People learn from what happens after someone speaks. If a leader invites questions and then mocks the first one, the invitation loses meaning. A constructive response acknowledges the contribution, checks its substance, and explains what will happen next. It need not agree with every claim or accept an unsupported suggestion.

In the practice form-review meeting, a staff member asks whether a mandatory field could exclude people without the requested document. The leader says the employee is always negative. That labels the person instead of examining the question. A useful response asks what evidence is available and who can verify the requirement.

The leader can state uncertainty and seek help without surrendering the decision. When the concern needs a formal complaint or other authority route, explain and use it. Do not absorb every report into ordinary group discussion. What matters is an appropriate response to the actual content, with professional treatment and clear follow-through.

In this lesson

1. Prepare a constructive response to a question that challenges a plan.

2. Distinguish content evaluation from a personal judgment about the contributor.

3. Identify a response that makes later input less likely.

4. What should the leader do?

The response tells the team whether the invitation was real.

Examine the decision

Acknowledge

Acknowledge the contribution without demanding that the person defend the right to raise it. In the field-requirement case, a brief thanks can reduce immediate dismissal. It must be followed by attention to the content; politeness alone does not examine whether the form has a real access problem.

Examine

Separate the question from the contributor’s presumed attitude. Ask whether the field is required, what alternatives exist, and which evidence or office can answer. If the suggestion is not feasible, explain the reason rather than describe the employee as negative or disloyal.

Next step

State who will check the issue, what can be shared, and when the team will revisit it. If the question involves a requirement outside the leader’s authority, route it properly. Saying “we will look at it” without responsibility can leave the concern parked indefinitely and make the invitation appear empty.

Option 4: Adopt the suggestion without checking the requirement.

The response treats the content seriously without replacing analysis or authority with automatic agreement.

Feedback for another response

Personal label

Calling the contributor negative can make the discussion seem efficient, but substitutes an attitude judgment for the missing information. Others may infer that challenging the plan carries a social penalty. Return to the specific question and evidence.

Constructive examination

Constructive examination can agree, disagree, or defer pending evidence. Its value is that the contribution receives a substantive response. Clear responsibility and a next review make uncertainty usable rather than leaving the person to interpret silence.

Polite dismissal

A polite thank-you followed by no examination can look welcoming while leaving the issue untouched. Treat the acknowledgment as the beginning. Explain whether the issue will be checked, why it is outside scope, or which route applies instead.

title: Learn from a mistake without replacing accountability
summary: Distinguish a learning review from a formal finding or discipline process.
body:
Distinguish a learning review from a formal finding or discipline process.

Colleagues share information and consider a decision together.

Examine how the work happened without promising that responsibility disappears.

Learn from a mistake without replacing accountability

When someone identifies a mistake, the team can examine how the work occurred and what needs improvement. That learning does not mean every error is acceptable or that formal accountability disappears. Different concerns require different procedures. A supervisor should not use a learning meeting to make a disciplinary finding or promise that no required response will occur.

In the practice form-review team, an outdated eligibility note reaches the draft because the source owner was unclear and the final check used a stale file. The team can correct the material and clarify the source-check responsibility. Blaming one person publicly may hide the process gap; refusing to discuss relevant responsibility leaves a different gap.

Separate the factual correction, learning question, and any formal matter requiring HR, legal, or other authority. Use approved information and avoid reproducing personal complaint or participant records. A useful learning review produces a specific change and follow-up, rather than a declaration that the team should celebrate every failure or punish every mistake.

In this lesson

1. Distinguish a learning review from a formal finding or discipline process.

2. Identify a process condition that contributed to a practice error.

3. Plan a proportionate improvement while preserving relevant responsibilities.

4. What is the better approach?

Examine how the work happened without promising that responsibility disappears.

Examine the decision

Work path

Trace the relevant handoffs and checks. In the outdated-note case, ask who maintained the source and which version was verified before drafting. This examines a workplace practice that can be changed. It does not excuse the error or establish that a particular person was solely responsible.

Separate responsibilities

A learning discussion asks what the process can improve; an authorized formal process addresses matters within its role. Some issues need both. Do not promise immunity or use the group meeting to decide discipline. Coordinate the appropriate route while keeping the process-learning question clear.

Repair and review

Correct the material and assign a source-check responsibility with a review point. Check whether the next draft uses the verified source. A new checklist is implementation evidence, not proof that every error is prevented. The improvement should be specific enough to test and proportionate to the actual problem.

Check your understanding

What is a useful response to the outdated eligibility note?

Option 1: Publicly assign blame without reviewing the handoff.

Option 2: Promise that no accountability can apply.

Option 3: Declare a new checklist prevents every future error.

Option 4: Correct it, examine the source-check process, and coordinate any formal responsibility separately.

Answer review

Correct response: Correct it, examine the source-check process, and coordinate any formal responsibility separately.

Feedback for the correct response

The response separates correction, learning, and proper authority while making an improvement reviewable.

Feedback for another response

Public blame may miss the workplace practices, while immunity promises can exceed authority. A checklist also cannot prove that all error is gone. Correct the material, examine the process, and keep formal responsibilities in the appropriate route.

Compare the approaches

Public blame

Public blame can produce an immediate explanation but discourages disclosure and may conceal the handoff gap. It is not a substitute for relevant accountability. Examine the work path and use formal procedures where required rather than inviting the group to assign fault.

No accountability

A promise of no accountability can make disclosure easier briefly but exceeds the leader’s authority and weakens expectations. Learning works better when boundaries are honest. Examine conditions and coordinate formal matters without pretending responsibility cannot apply.

Learning with boundaries

Learning with boundaries corrects the work, examines conditions, and preserves proper authority. It gives the team an actionable improvement without deciding matters outside the discussion. Review its use and limits rather than declare that one repair solves all risk.

title: Recognize hierarchy and keep the right concern routes open
summary: Identify a power difference that can affect willingness to speak.
body:
Identify a power difference that can affect willingness to speak.

Colleagues share information and consider a decision together.

An open-door statement is not enough when the leader controls opportunity.

Recognize hierarchy and keep the right concern routes open

The leader who invites input may also control assignments, evaluations, and development. Staff can reasonably consider those consequences before disagreeing. An open-door statement is useful only when the response and available routes support it. Do not assume that silence from a newer employee means the employee has no concern.

In the practice form-review team, a temporary staff member sees an access problem but expects public disagreement with the project lead to harm future assignments. A prepared written route or an appropriate private conversation may make the contribution more usable. It should not require the person to explain personal history or speak on behalf of a whole group.

An ordinary design question can belong in the team’s decision process. An allegation of discrimination or another formal concern needs its proper route and duties. Do not keep it in the learning space or require the person to confront the supervisor first. The consultant can support thinking and capability, but should not become a permission gate for reporting.

In this lesson

1. Identify a power difference that can affect willingness to speak.

2. Plan an input route that does not depend on public confrontation with a supervisor.

3. Distinguish an ordinary design concern from a report requiring a formal response.

4. What should the leader do?

An open-door statement is not enough when the leader controls opportunity.

Examine the decision

Power

Consider who controls opportunity and whose contribution carries more risk. In the temporary-staff case, the leader may experience the question as routine while the staff member sees an assignment consequence. Recognizing that difference helps the leader design the route without claiming to know every person’s feelings.

Alternative

Offer a route that reaches the decision without forced public confrontation. A focused written question or an appropriate private contact can help. Confirm who reviews it and what influence remains possible. Do not offer a supposedly anonymous route unless its privacy and technical limits are actually established.

Formal concern

The substance of the concern determines whether a formal route is needed. If a report alleges protected-class harassment, the leader’s reporting responsibilities remain. A team-learning invitation cannot hold the allegation privately as a simulation or wait for consultant approval before the person or area responsible is contacted.

Option 1: Provide usable input routes and accurate boundaries while preserving formal reporting access.

Option 2: Treat silence as proof of no concern.

Option 3: Require public confrontation with the supervisor.

Option 4: Promise anonymity without knowing the route’s limits.

Answer review

Correct response: Provide usable input routes and accurate boundaries while preserving formal reporting access.

Feedback for the correct response

The response acknowledges power differences through practical access rather than unsupported guarantees.

Feedback for another response

Silence, forced confrontation, and an unverified anonymity promise can each hide a participation barrier. Explain usable routes and their limits, and keep formal reporting available without requiring a team-learning conversation first.

Compare the approaches

Open door only

An open-door statement is easy to make but may still leave staff dependent on confronting the person who controls their work. Pair it with usable routes, accurate limits, and professional responses. Do not use lack of visitors as evidence that no concerns exist.

Usable route with limits

A usable route identifies the contact, timing, purpose, and information limits. It can give staff a practical alternative while preserving authority. Avoid an unverified anonymity promise and explain which concerns require another formal process.

Team-only rule

A team-only rule may be framed as keeping learning collaborative, but can block formal reporting access and necessary duties. Distinguish the design discussion from a complaint. Use the proper route without making the reporter complete a group conversation first.
